questions.title: Death from disease progression after a properly performed operation
questions.question: A 12-year-old child with a history of rheumatic heart was admitted to hospital for tonsillectomy; he was operated on after full preoperative counseling and was discharged from hospital 2 days later. One month later, he developed heart failure and was readmitted to the hospital, but unfortunately, he passed away despite of clinical care. Can the parent sue the ENT doctor?

options.A: Yes, he can sue him for incompetence.
options.B: Yes, he can sue him for negligence.
options.C: Yes, he can sue him for medical error.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Incompetence means a lack of reasonable skill or knowledge, and nothing in the scenario shows the ENT surgeon lacked either — the operation and counselling were properly done.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Negligence requires a breach of the standard of care that caused the harm, but here the care met the standard and the death came from progression of the pre-existing rheumatic heart disease.
explanations.C: Incorrect. There is no medical error to point to: the surgery and perioperative care were appropriate, and a later cardiac death is an outcome of the underlying disease, not a mistake.
explanations.D: Correct. The parent cannot sue, because a bad outcome that follows proper care is not actionable — liability needs fault (negligence or incompetence) that caused the harm. Here the tonsillectomy was correctly performed with full counselling, and the fatal heart failure a month later reflects the child's underlying rheumatic heart disease rather than any breach of duty. An adverse result on its own, without a proven breach of the standard of care, is not malpractice.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that a poor outcome following proper care, from progression of the underlying disease, is not grounds for a malpractice suit.

questions.title: Basis of liability for an incompatible blood transfusion
questions.question: In case of incompatible blood transfusion, the doctor is liable to be sued because of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Incompetence is a lack of reasonable skill or knowledge; checking compatibility before transfusion is basic expected practice, so the failure here is a lapse in care, not a lack of competence.
explanations.B: Correct. Giving an incompatible transfusion is negligence, because the doctor failed to carry out the standard, expected safeguard of confirming blood-group compatibility before transfusing. Negligence is a breach of the duty of care that a reasonably careful doctor would have honoured, and the resulting harm makes the doctor liable. The error is one of careless practice rather than absent knowledge or an ethical offence.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Misconduct denotes ethical or disciplinary violations (e.g. dishonesty, immoral behaviour), not a careless clinical failure such as omitting a compatibility check.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A dispensing error refers to the pharmacy step of supplying a medication; a mismatched transfusion is a failure of the transfusion-safety duty, categorised as negligence.

questions.learning_objective: Identify an incompatible blood transfusion as negligence for which the doctor is liable.

questions.title: Definition of incompetence
questions.question: Lack of reasonable skills or knowledge is defined as:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Assault is causing a person to fear imminent harmful contact (in the medical context, contact without consent); it has nothing to do with the level of a doctor's skill or knowledge.
explanations.B: Correct. Incompetence is defined as a lack of the reasonable skill or knowledge expected of a practitioner. It describes a deficiency in ability or learning, in contrast to negligence, which is a careless failure to apply the care one is capable of. Naming the deficiency of skill/knowledge as incompetence is the distinction this item tests.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Malpractice is the broad term for professional wrongdoing that harms a patient; it is the umbrella under which negligence and incompetence sit, not the specific definition of lacking skill or knowledge.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Negligence is a breach of the standard of care — failing to do what a reasonably careful doctor would do — rather than a lack of the underlying skill or knowledge itself.

questions.learning_objective: Define incompetence as a lack of reasonable skill or knowledge.

questions.title: What must be proved in every malpractice case
questions.question: The following must be proved in every medical malpractice case:

options.C: Negligence or incompetence that lead to patient's harm

explanations.A: Incorrect. Negligence alone is not enough; even a clear breach of care is not actionable malpractice unless it actually caused the patient harm.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Incompetence alone is likewise insufficient; the deficiency must be shown to have led to harm before a malpractice claim can succeed.
explanations.C: Correct. Every malpractice case must prove a fault — negligence or incompetence — AND that this fault caused harm to the patient. Fault without resulting harm, or harm without fault, does not establish malpractice; the two must be linked by causation. This requirement of fault-plus-harm is the core element the question tests.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "All of the above" would require both negligence and incompetence together, but the case needs either one that causes harm, which is exactly what option C states.

questions.learning_objective: State that malpractice requires proof of negligence or incompetence that caused patient harm.

questions.title: Breach of duty when a head-trauma patient is sent home
questions.question: A 50-year-old female patient suffering from a severe head trauma was admitted to the emergency room. After examination, the doctor assured her that she is in a good condition and needs no admission. Few hours later, she suffered from headache and vomiting. She was then admitted to the hospital but unfortunately, she lost consciousness and died. What is the breach of duty that occurred?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Abandonment is ending the doctor-patient relationship without notice or arrangement for continued care; here the doctor did not abandon her but failed to admit and observe her.
explanations.B: Incorrect. An act of commission is a wrong act actually performed; the fault here was not doing something indicated (admission/observation), not a wrong act carried out.
explanations.C: Correct. Failing to admit and observe a patient with severe head trauma who needed monitoring is a failure to do something that should have been done — an act (error) of omission. The indicated step of admission for observation was omitted, and the deterioration and death followed from that omission. Omission errors are failures to act, in contrast to commission errors, which are wrong acts performed.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Unnecessary treatment means giving care that was not indicated; the problem here was the opposite — necessary admission and observation were withheld.

questions.learning_objective: Classify a failure to admit and observe an at-risk patient as a breach of duty by omission.

questions.title: Which act is not malpractice — the emergency-consent exception
questions.question: A doctor could be accused of malpractice for many reasons, which of the following acts isn't considered malpractice?

options.A: Failure to take patient's operative consent in an emergency condition
options.B: Immoral conduct in the practice of profession
options.C: Improper preoperative preparation that leads to complication

explanations.A: Correct. In a genuine emergency, when the patient cannot consent and delay would risk life or serious harm, consent is presumed and treating without formal consent is lawful — so failure to take operative consent in an emergency is not malpractice. Emergency care is the recognised exception to the consent requirement. The other options are all genuine grounds for a malpractice accusation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Immoral conduct in professional practice is professional misconduct and is a legitimate basis for a malpractice/disciplinary accusation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Improper preoperative preparation that leads to a complication is a failure of the standard of care and can amount to malpractice.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Misuse of drug prescription is a clear deviation from safe practice and may be malpractice.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that failing to obtain consent in a genuine emergency is not malpractice.

questions.title: Failing to use expected skill and injuring the patient
questions.question: If a physician fails to use a degree of skill and learning commonly expected and the person receiving care is injured, the physician can be sued for ______.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Assault and battery involve threatening or making contact without consent; the scenario is about a shortfall in professional skill, not unconsented contact.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Indecency is a moral/behavioural offence and does not describe a failure to apply commonly expected clinical skill.
explanations.C: Correct. When a physician fails to use the degree of skill and learning commonly expected and the patient is thereby injured, that is malpractice — the broad term for professional wrongdoing causing patient harm. Malpractice is the umbrella that covers both negligence (careless practice) and incompetence (lack of skill/knowledge) once harm results. Because the item pairs a failure of expected skill with an actual injury, the general charge is malpractice.
explanations.D: Incorrect (close distractor). Negligence is one form of malpractice, but the phrasing here — failing to use commonly expected skill and learning causing injury — describes the overall charge of malpractice rather than the specific sub-type.

questions.learning_objective: Identify failure to use commonly expected skill that injures the patient as malpractice.

questions.title: Which example is NOT medical negligence
questions.question: Which one of the following examples is NOT considered medical negligence?

options.B: Failure to obtain consent for surgical procedure.
options.D: Performing CPR for arrested patient in the street.

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS negligence). Transfusing without cross-matching omits a basic compatibility safeguard and is negligence.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS negligence). Failing to obtain consent for a (non-emergency) surgical procedure breaches the duty to inform and is negligence.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this IS negligence). Medication errors are careless failures of safe prescribing/administration and count as negligence.
explanations.D: Correct. Performing CPR on a stranger who has arrested in the street is emergency aid where no prior doctor-patient relationship (and hence no pre-existing legal duty of care) existed, so it is not medical negligence. Negligence presupposes a duty of care that was breached; a bystander rendering good-faith emergency help is not held to that professional duty. This is why the street-CPR example is the one that is not negligence.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that good-faith emergency aid to a stranger, with no pre-existing duty, is not medical negligence.

questions.title: Which example IS medical negligence
questions.question: Which one of the following examples is considered medical negligence?

options.B: Failure to obtain consent for surgical procedure
options.D: Performing CPR for an arrested patient without consent

explanations.A: Incorrect. Transfusing after proper cross-matching is correct, safe practice, not negligence.
explanations.B: Correct. Failing to obtain informed consent before a (non-emergency) surgical procedure is medical negligence, because informing the patient and securing consent is a required duty owed before operating. Omitting it breaches the standard of care and exposes the patient to an unauthorised procedure. Consent is only dispensed with in a genuine emergency, which this option does not describe.
explanations.C: Incorrect (as the single best answer). Prescribing a non-registered remedy is improper and may be professional misconduct or a regulatory offence, but the example the item marks as negligence is the failure to obtain surgical consent.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Performing CPR on an arrested patient without waiting for consent is appropriate emergency care (consent is presumed when life is at risk), not negligence.

questions.learning_objective: Identify failure to obtain consent for a non-emergency surgical procedure as medical negligence.

questions.title: Cause of death in a haemolytic transfusion reaction
questions.question: Death in hemolytic blood transfusion may occur due to:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Adrenal failure is not the mechanism of death in a haemolytic transfusion reaction.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Although haemolysis releases bilirubin and can cause jaundice, death is not from hepatic failure.
explanations.C: Correct. In a haemolytic (incompatible) transfusion reaction, the massive breakdown of red cells releases free haemoglobin that, with hypotension and disseminated intravascular coagulation, precipitates acute renal failure — the usual cause of death. Pigment (haemoglobin) nephropathy and shock damage the kidneys. Renal failure is therefore the classic fatal complication of an incompatible transfusion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Respiratory failure is not the characteristic fatal pathway of a haemolytic transfusion reaction.

questions.learning_objective: State that death in a haemolytic transfusion reaction occurs through acute renal failure.

questions.title: Anaesthesiologist's duty before administering anaesthesia
questions.question: Before anesthesia is administered, the anesthesiologist has to:

options.B: Meet the patient at the operating room.
options.C: Ignore data not related directly to the operation.

explanations.A: Correct. Before administering anaesthesia the anaesthesiologist must examine (assess) the patient thoroughly — a full pre-anaesthetic evaluation of history, airway, comorbidities and investigations. This preoperative assessment is the duty that identifies risks and prevents avoidable anaesthetic harm. Skipping it is a breach of the standard of care.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The patient should be assessed beforehand, not first met in the operating room; meeting the patient only at induction leaves no time for proper evaluation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The anaesthesiologist must not ignore medical data unrelated to the operation, because comorbidities not directly connected to the surgery still affect anaesthetic risk.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Agitation is not a reason to refuse care; it should be assessed and managed, not used to decline the patient.

questions.module_subject: 327 MPE > Medical Professionalism & Ethics > Patient safety > Anaesthesia safety
questions.learning_objective: State that the anaesthesiologist must examine the patient thoroughly before administering anaesthesia.

questions.title: Proper defence when a patient unilaterally left the doctor's care
questions.question: A patient with diabetic foot left his physician to another one without any declaration. After few months, the patient raised a claim against the first doctor accusing him that his treatment resulted into gangrene and amputation of his foot. What is the proper response of the doctor in this situation?

options.A: Deny his relation with the patient
options.C: Tell the court that the patient did not follow the instructions of the course of the treatment.
options.D: Tell the court that the patient dismissed him suddenly.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Denying the doctor-patient relationship would be dishonest and is easily disproved by the records; it is not an honest or effective defence.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Engaging a lawyer is a practical step but is not the substantive answer to the claim; it does not address why the doctor is not responsible for the later course.
explanations.C: Incorrect (weaker). Non-adherence may be relevant, but the decisive fact is that the patient himself ended the relationship without notice, which is what relieves the first doctor of responsibility for the subsequent deterioration.
explanations.D: Correct. The proper response is to tell the court that the patient dismissed him suddenly — the patient unilaterally terminated the doctor-patient relationship without declaration and moved to another physician. Once the patient ends the relationship, the first doctor no longer has a continuing duty for the later course of the disease, so he is not responsible for the subsequent gangrene and amputation. Truthfully stating that the patient discharged him is therefore the honest and legally sound defence.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that a patient who unilaterally ends care relieves the doctor of duty for the later course, which is the doctor's proper defence.

questions.title: Obligations of doctors
questions.question: Doctors have an obligation to:

options.B: Rescuing persons who are in danger.

explanations.A: Incorrect as the single best answer. Helping individuals with disabilities is a genuine obligation, but it is only one of the duties listed.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the single best answer. Rescuing persons in danger is a real duty, yet it is one of several listed obligations.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the single best answer. Preventing and removing harm (beneficence and non-maleficence) is a core duty, but again only one of the options.
explanations.D: Correct. Doctors' professional obligations include helping people with disabilities, rescuing those in danger, and preventing and removing harm, so all of the listed duties apply and the complete answer is "all of the above". Each option reflects the ethical duties of beneficence and non-maleficence expected of the profession. Because every one is a genuine obligation, no single option is sufficient on its own.

questions.learning_objective: List helping the disabled, rescuing those in danger, and preventing/removing harm as doctors' obligations.

questions.title: A feature of an incompatible blood transfusion
questions.question: Incompatible blood transfusion may cause one of the following:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cyanosis reflects deoxygenation and is not the characteristic feature of an incompatible transfusion reaction.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Flushing can occur in some transfusion reactions but is not the hallmark of a haemolytic incompatibility.
explanations.C: Correct. An incompatible blood transfusion causes intravascular haemolysis, and the breakdown of red cells releases bilirubin, which produces jaundice. The same haemolysis underlies the free-haemoglobin load that can damage the kidneys. Jaundice is therefore the listed feature that follows from the haemolytic reaction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Pallor suggests anaemia or shock in general and is not the specific sign of the haemolysis of an incompatible transfusion.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise jaundice (from haemolysis) as a feature of an incompatible blood transfusion.

questions.title: Medical mistakes liable to a malpractice lawsuit — the exception
questions.question: The following are medical mistakes liable to malpractice lawsuit, except:

options.B: Brain damage of new born due to hypoxia from prolonged labor.
options.D: Over tight plaster cast causing tissue and nerve damage.

explanations.A: Correct. An unsuccessful operation is the exception, because a poor result on its own is not malpractice — a bad outcome can occur despite entirely correct care, and liability needs a proven fault that caused harm. The other options each describe a preventable, fault-based injury. Absent negligence or incompetence, an operation that simply fails is not actionable.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS liable). Neonatal brain damage from hypoxia due to mishandled prolonged labour reflects a failure of intrapartum care and can be malpractice.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this IS liable). Diathermy burns are a preventable technical injury and are grounds for a malpractice claim.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this IS liable). An over-tight plaster cast causing tissue and nerve damage is a careless, preventable harm and is actionable.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that an unsuccessful operation without fault is not, by itself, malpractice.

questions.title: Against whom a malpractice claim is raised
questions.question: A claim of malpractice is raised upon:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The hospital may bear vicarious institutional liability, but the malpractice claim itself is directed at the practitioner whose professional act is in question.
explanations.B: Correct. A claim of medical malpractice is raised upon the physician, because malpractice concerns the professional duty and conduct of the individual doctor whose act or omission caused the harm. It is the physician's personal breach of the standard of care that is adjudicated. Others may share liability separately, but the malpractice claim targets the physician.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Nursing staff answer for their own nursing acts; a physician's malpractice claim is not raised upon the nurses.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Technicians are responsible for their own technical duties, not for the physician's malpractice.

questions.learning_objective: State that a malpractice claim is raised upon the physician.

questions.title: When a malpractice action cannot be raised — no harm
questions.question: Action of malpractice may be raised in the following conditions, except:

options.A: Renal failure due to incompatible blood transfusion.
options.C: Leaving instrument in the abdominal cavity without damage.
options.D: Toxicity by overdose of prescribed medication.

explanations.A: Incorrect (an action CAN be raised). Renal failure from an incompatible transfusion is a fault that caused real harm and is actionable.
explanations.B: Incorrect (an action CAN be raised). An abscess from an unsterilised injection is a preventable injury and is actionable.
explanations.C: Correct. Leaving an instrument in the abdominal cavity WITHOUT causing any damage is the exception, because malpractice requires that the fault actually caused harm — with no resulting damage there is no compensable injury to sue over. The retained instrument is certainly a fault, but absent harm the malpractice action fails on the damage element. This illustrates that fault without harm is not actionable malpractice.
explanations.D: Incorrect (an action CAN be raised). Toxicity from an overdose of a prescribed medication is a harmful, fault-based error and is actionable.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that without resulting harm (a retained instrument causing no damage) a malpractice action cannot be raised.

questions.title: Acts regarded as medical negligence
questions.question: Which of the following act by a medical man can be regarded as an act of medical negligence?

options.A: Modifying the operative procedure beyond the permitted scope.
options.B: Not informing the patient about the complication of the operation.
options.C: Not taking the consent of the patient before operation.

explanations.A: Incorrect as the single best answer. Exceeding the permitted scope of the agreed procedure is negligence, but it is only one of the listed acts.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the single best answer. Failing to inform the patient of operative complications breaches the duty to disclose, yet it is one of several listed acts.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the single best answer. Operating without the patient's consent is negligence, but again only one of the options.
explanations.D: Correct. Modifying a procedure beyond the permitted scope, not disclosing operative complications, and operating without consent are all breaches of the duty of care, so each is an act of medical negligence and the complete answer is "all of the above". Every listed act departs from what a reasonably careful doctor owes the patient. Because all three qualify, no single option is sufficient.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise exceeding scope, non-disclosure of complications, and operating without consent as acts of negligence.

questions.title: Negligence reflects inadequacy of what
questions.question: A physician is convicted of medical negligence due to inadequacy of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Inadequate scientific knowledge is the mark of incompetence, not negligence.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A deficiency of manual and technical skill likewise describes incompetence rather than negligence.
explanations.C: Correct. Negligence is a conviction for inadequacy of medical CARE — a careless failure to apply the attention and diligence a competent doctor would give, even though the knowledge and skill were present. It contrasts with incompetence, which is an inadequacy of knowledge or skill itself. The distinguishing feature of negligence is the lapse in the standard of care, not a lack of ability.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Inadequacy of professional behaviour points to professional misconduct (an ethical/disciplinary category), not to negligence.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish negligence (inadequacy of medical care) from incompetence (inadequacy of knowledge/skill).
